title: Vailankanni (India)
hook: a coastal shrine of Our Lady of Good Health, loved by people of many religions

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kibeho: visions in Rwanda, and a lady who called herself Mother of the Word. Your line was mother of the word. Did your words go easier on someone? Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

On the beach, a woman in a yellow sari is making her way toward a white church on her knees. Behind her, a father carries a little boy whose head has just been shaved, an offering for a fever that broke. At a stall nearby, someone is buying a small wax model of a leg, to leave at the altar for a knee that won't heal. Some of the pilgrims are Catholic. Some are Hindu. Some are Muslim. They've all come to the same shore in the south of India, to a mother they call by one name: Our Lady of Good Health. Today's word is the town on that coast.
screen: `ON HER KNEES TOWARD A WHITE CHURCH.` → `A WAX LEG FOR A BAD KNEE.` → `ONE SHORE, PILGRIMS OF MANY FAITHS.`

segments.voice: Start with the stories, which come from tradition rather than any record. Tradition says a boy carrying milk to a customer stopped to rest under a tree, and a beautiful lady holding a child asked him for milk for her son. He gave it, and arrived to find his pot still full. Another story tells of a lame boy selling buttermilk who was asked the same, gave, and stood up and walked. And sailors caught in a storm off the coast are said to have promised Mary a chapel if they reached land alive. They did, and they built it. Notice what holds these stories together: a mother asking for something for her child, and people being healed and kept safe. Next, the name. In the Litany of Loreto, Mary is called health of the sick. Vailankanni gives her almost that title: Our Lady of Good Health. People come here carrying their bodies: bad backs, failing eyes, children who won't eat, babies they've long hoped for. They bring wax or metal models of the part that hurts and leave them as a kind of prayer you can hold in your hand. That instinct is old. In Matthew's Gospel, a sick woman pushes through a crowd toward Jesus, thinking, in the Douay-Rheims: "If I shall touch only his garment, I shall be healed." She wanted to bring her body close. Last, the neighbors. The shrine's gates stand open to anyone, and people of other faiths come to pray there too, in their own ways. Catholics there don't check anyone at the door. They meet them as fellow pilgrims, all asking for the same plain thing.
screen: `A MOTHER ASKS FOR MILK.` · `HEALTH OF THE SICK.` · `BRINGING THE BODY CLOSE.` · `OPEN TO NEIGHBORS.` · then, large: `IF I SHALL TOUCH ONLY HIS GARMENT, I SHALL BE HEALED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for good health. Settle, and breathe. Start with your own body. Find one part of it that works today without your asking: lungs, hands, eyes. Rest your attention there for a few breaths. Then find one part that hurts or worries you, and don't argue with it. Just notice it. Now let your mind travel to someone whose health is failing, and hold them as gently as you just held yourself. If you pray, you can say a Hail Mary for them, or the litany's words, health of the sick, pray for us. If you don't, simply wish them well, by name. The bell holds the time.
Vailankanni. The town on India's southern coast where Mary is honored as Our Lady of Good Health, and pilgrims of many faiths come asking to be healed. Today's word.
Your line: our lady of good health. Today, do one plain thing for someone's health: a glass of water, a walk together, a ride to the doctor. Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Pilgrims come to the Basilica of Our Lady of Good Health at Vailankanni in Tamil Nadu, India, to pray for healing, some walking on their knees or offering small models of the part of the body they hope to see healed; people of other faiths visit and pray there too.

notes: Editor: one change: no longer says pilgrims of other faiths are all asking 'the same mother', which spoke for them.

The three founding stories (a Hindu milk boy, a lame buttermilk seller healed, Portuguese sailors saved in a storm who built a chapel) are told as tradition, without dates or names. Confirm the details (e.g. the pot staying full; the boy's lameness healed).
Pilgrim customs in the hook and teach (walking on knees, head-shaving as a vow, offering wax or metal models of body parts): confirm these are practiced at Vailankanni.
That Hindu and Muslim pilgrims come is stated from the index ('loved by people of many religions'); confirm. The script describes them as fellow pilgrims and makes no comparison.
The Tamil title (often Arokia Matha / Aarokya Annai) is not used in the voice; confirm whether to add it.
'babies they've long hoped for' is a general example of what pilgrims bring; confirm acceptable.
